source_text: Coronant et publicos ordines laureis publicae caussae, magistratus vero insuper aureis. Superferuntur etiam illis Hetruscae. Hoc vocabulum est coronarum, quas gemmis et foliis ex auro quercinis ob Jovem insignis ad deducendas thensas cum palmatis togis sumunt. Sunt et provinciales aureae, imaginum jam, non virorum, capita majora quaerentes. Sed tui ordines et tui magistratus, et ipsum curiae nomen Ecclesia est Christi. Illius es conscriptus in libris vitae. Illic purpurae tuae sanguis Domini et clavus latus in cruce ipsius; illic securis ad caudicem arboris posita, illic virgae ex Jesse. Viderint et publici equi cum coronis suis. Dominus tuus, ubi secundum Scripturam Jerusalem ingredi voluit, nec asinum habuit privatum. Isti in curribus et isti in equis, nos autem in nomine Domini Dei nostri invocabimus. Ab ipso incolatu Babylonis illius in Apocalypsi Joannis submovemur, nedum a suggestu. Coronatur et vulgus nunc ex principalium prosperitatum exultatione, nunc ex municipalium solemnitatum proprietate: et est omnis publicae laetitiae luxuria captatrix. Sed tu peregrinus mundi hujus, civis supernae Jerusalem. Noster, inquit, municipatus in coelis. Habes tuos sensus, tuos fastos: nihil tibi cum gaudiis saeculi; imo contrarium debes: Saeculum enim gaudebit, vos vero lugebitis. Et puto, felices ait lugentes, non coronatos. Coronant et nuptiae sponsos, ideo non nubamus ethnicis, ne nos ad idolatriam usque deducant, a qua apud illos nuptiae incipiunt: habes legem a Patriarchis quidem, habes apostolum in Domino nubere jubentem. Coronat et libertas saecularis. Sed tu jam redemptus es a Christo, et quidem magno. Servum alienum quomodo saeculum manumittet? Etsi libertas videtur, sed et servitus videbatur. Omnia imaginaria in saeculo, et nihil veri. Nam et tunc liber hominis eras redemptus a Christo: et nunc servus es Christi, licet manumissus ab homine. Si veram putes saeculi libertatem, ut et corona consignes, rediisti in servitutem hominis, quam putes libertatem; amisisti libertatem Christi, quam putas servitutem. Numquid et agonisticae caussae disputabuntur, quas statim tituli sui damnant? et sacras et funebres scilicet, hoc enim superest ut Olympius Jupiter, et Nemaeus Hercules, et misellus Archemorus, et Antinous infelix in Christiano coronentur, ut ipse spectaculum fiat, quod spectare debet. Universas, ut arbitror, caussas enumeravimus. Nec ulla nobiscum est: omnes alienae, profanae, illicitae, semel jam in sacramenti testatione ejeratae. Haec enim erant pompae diaboli et angelorum ejus officia, saeculi honores, solemnitates, popularitates, falsa vota, humana servitia, laudes vanae, gloriae turpes: et in omnibus istis idololatria, in solo quoque sensu coronarum quibus omnia ista redimita sunt. Praefabitur quidem Claudius etiam coelum sideribus apud Homeri carmina coronatum; certe a Deo, certe homini, igitur et homo ipse a Deo coronandus est. Caeterum a saeculo coronantur et lupanaria, et latrinae, et pistrina, et carcer, et ludus, et ipsa amphitheatra, et ipsa spoliaria, ipsaeque libitinae. Quam sacer sanctus, quamque honestus ac mundus sit habitus iste, noli de uno poetico coelo, sed de totius mundi commerciis aestimare. At enim Christianus nec januam suam laureis infamabit, si norit quantos deos etiam ostiis diabolus affinxerit, Janum a janua, Limentinum a limine, Forculum et Cardam a foribus et cardinibus et apud Graecos Thyreum Apollinem et Antelios daemonas.
pass_a_gloss: They crown also public orders with laurels for public causes, but magistrates indeed with golden ones. Also Etruscan things are placed upon them. This word is of crowns, which with gems and leaves of oak from gold, notable because of Jupiter, they take for leading out processions with palmated togas. There are also provincial golden ones, now seeking larger images of men, not of men. But your orders and your magistrates, and the very name of the senate is the Church of Christ. You are enrolled in the books of life of Him. There your purple is the blood of the Lord and the nail in the side on the cross of Him; there the axe is placed at the trunk of the tree, there the rods from Jesse. Let them see also the public horses with their crowns. Your Lord, where according to Scripture He wanted to enter Jerusalem, did not have a private donkey. These in chariots and these on horses, but we will invoke in the name of the Lord our God. We are removed from the dwelling of that Babylon in the Apocalypse of John, much less from the tribunal. The crowd is also crowned now from the exultation of principal prosperities, now from the property of municipal solemnities: and every luxury of public joy is captivating. But you are a stranger of this world, a citizen of the heavenly Jerusalem. Our municipality, it says, is in the heavens. You have your own senses, your own festivals: nothing to you with the joys of the age; indeed the opposite you ought: for the age will rejoice, but you will mourn. And I think, He says, blessed are those mourning, not crowned. Weddings also crown the betrothed, therefore we do not marry pagans, lest they lead us to idolatry, from which weddings begin among them: you have the law from the Patriarchs, you have the apostle commanding to marry in the Lord. Secular freedom also crowns. But you are already redeemed by Christ, and indeed at a great price. How will the secular world free a foreign slave? Even if freedom seems, but also servitude seems. All things are imaginary in the world, and nothing true. For even then you were a free man redeemed by Christ: and now you are a slave of Christ, although freed by man. If you think the freedom of the world is true, so that you also ratify the crown, you have returned to the servitude of man, which you think is freedom; you have lost the freedom of Christ, which you think is servitude. Will perhaps also agonistic causes be disputed, which their titles immediately condemn? And sacred and funeral ones, certainly, for this remains that Olympian Jupiter, and Nemean Hercules, and wretched Archemorus, and unfortunate Antinous be crowned in a Christian, so that he himself becomes a spectacle, which he ought to watch. I think we have enumerated all causes. And none is with us: all are foreign, profane, illicit, once already rejected in the testimony of the sacrament. For these were the pomp of the devil and the offices of his angels, the honors of the world, solemnities, popularities, false vows, human servitudes, empty praises, shameful glories: and in all these idolatry, in the sole sense of crowns with which all these are adorned. Certainly Claudius also crowns the heaven with stars in the songs of Homer; certainly by God, certainly by man, therefore man himself is to be crowned by God. Moreover, from the world brothels and latrines and bakeries and prison and game and the very amphitheaters and the very spoliariums and the very funeral pyres are crowned. How sacred and holy and honest and pure is this habit, do not estimate from one poetic heaven, but from the commerce of the whole world. But indeed a Christian will not defile his door with laurels, if he knows how many gods the devil has also fixed on doors, Janus from the door, Limentinus from the threshold, Forculus and Cardam from the doors and hinges, and among the Greeks Thyreus Apollo and Antelios demons.
pass_b_english: They crown public officials with laurels for the public good, but magistrates receive gold crowns. Etruscan regalia are heaped on top of those. The very word for these crowns — wrought from gold oak leaves and gems, marked out for Jupiter — means they are worn to lead processions in palm-bordered togas. There are also provincial gold crowns, and these no longer seek likenesses of men; they demand larger-than-life images. But your ranks, your magistrates, the very name of your senate — that is the Church of Christ. You are enrolled in the books of life of the Lamb. There your purple is the blood of the Lord, the nail driven in His side on the cross; there the axe lies at the tree's root; there are the rods from Jesse. Let the state horses parade with their crowns. Your Lord, when He chose to enter Jerusalem according to Scripture, did not even own a donkey. They trust in chariots and horses; we will invoke the name of the Lord our God. We have been removed from the dwelling of that Babylon in the Apocalypse of John (Rev 17–18), let alone from the tribunal. The mob gets crowned too — now for the triumph of great victories, now for the pageant of municipal festivals — and every luxury of public joy is a trap. But you are a stranger in this world, a citizen of the heavenly Jerusalem. As it says, our citizenship is in heaven (Phil 3:20). You have your own instincts, your own calendar; you have nothing to do with the world's joys. On the contrary: the world will rejoice, but you will mourn. And I think, He says, blessed are those who mourn, not those who are crowned (Matt 5:4). Weddings crown the betrothed, which is why we do not marry pagans — lest they drag us into idolatry, from which their weddings begin. You have the law from the Patriarchs, you have the apostle commanding marriage in the Lord (1 Cor 7:39). Secular freedom also hands out crowns. But you have already been redeemed by Christ, and at a great price. How can the world free a slave who belongs to another? Freedom may appear, but servitude also appears. Everything in the world is imaginary; nothing is true. Even then you were a free man redeemed by Christ; now you are Christ's slave, though freed by a man. If you take the world's freedom as real and ratify its crown, you have returned to the slavery of man — which you call freedom — and lost the freedom of Christ — which you call slavery. Will athletic contests also be debated, when their very titles condemn them? Sacred and funeral games too — for that would mean Olympian Jupiter, Nemean Hercules, wretched Archemorus, and unhappy Antinous get crowned on a Christian, so that he becomes the spectacle he ought to be watching. I think we have listed every occasion. Not one belongs to us; all are foreign, profane, illicit, already renounced in the sacrament's testimony. Those were the devil's pomp, the offices of his angels: worldly honors, solemnities, popularity contests, false vows, human slaveries, empty praises, shameful glories — and idolatry in all of it, concentrated in the very meaning of the crowns that bind them together. Claudius even claims heaven is crowned with stars in Homer's songs; whether by God or by man, therefore man himself must be crowned by God. Meanwhile, the world crowns brothels, latrines, bakeries, prisons, games, the amphitheaters themselves, the corpse-pits, the funeral pyres. Do not judge the sanctity of this habit by one poetic heaven; judge it by the commerce of the whole world. And a Christian will not defile his own door with laurels, if he knows how many gods the devil has nailed to doorways: Janus from the door, Limentinus from the threshold, Forculus and Cardea from the leaves and hinges, and among the Greeks, Thyreus Apollo and the Antelios demons.

review.notes: Pass A fails on agency and completeness regarding the description of the crowns. The Latin 'quas gemmis et foliis ex auro quercinis ob Jovem insignis ad deducendas thensas cum palmatis togis sumunt' describes crowns made of gold oak leaves and gems, notable for Jupiter, which are taken/used for leading processions. Pass A translates 'insignis' as 'notable', but fails to capture the syntactic link that the crowns themselves are the objects being used ('sumunt') for the processions. More critically, Pass A translates 'imaginum jam, non virorum, capita majora quaerentes' as 'now seeking larger images of men, not of men', which is a logical contradiction/error; the Latin means they seek larger heads (capita) of images (imaginum), rather than heads of men. Pass B is much better but the failure of Pass A on the 'imaginum' clause necessitates a fail. Additionally, Pass A translates 'secundum Scripturam Jerusalem ingredi voluit' as 'where according to Scripture He wanted to enter Jerusalem', whereas the Latin 'voluit' (wished/intended) is better rendered as 'He intended to enter' or 'He chose to enter', though 'wanted' is acceptable; however, the 'imaginum' error is a substantive failure of sense.
reasons: Pass A: 'now seeking larger images of men, not of men' is a nonsensical translation of 'imaginum jam, non virorum, capita majora quaerentes' (seeking larger heads of images, not of men).
